prompt.context: Our client owns a designer shoe store that makes high-end, made-to-measure shoes for customers. The high-quality product has gained popularity rapidly and the client wants to ramp up production. However, the highly skilled labor that the client employs is hard to come by.
prompt.question: The client wants us to help them figure out how to increase output without adversely affecting quality. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: Are there additional skilled shoemakers available in the market?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are no additional skilled shoemakers available.

clarifying_info.q: What does the shoemaking process look like?
clarifying_info.a: The shoe-making process has 3 stages: cutting, stitching, and finishing.

clarifying_info.q: How many workers are there and how long does it take to make a pair?
clarifying_info.a: There are currently 15 workers, each of whom takes an average of 12 hours to produce one pair of shoes.

clarifying_info.q: Does each worker perform all three steps?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, each shoemaker currently performs all three steps of the process.

clarifying_info.q: Do all workers have the same skill sets across the three tasks?
clarifying_info.a: No, different shoemakers have different skill sets. [Hand the candidate Exhibit 1.]

clarifying_info.q: Can the process be changed so that shoemakers perform only specific tasks?
Is there any technology available to boost output?
clarifying_info.a: No, there is currently no technology we can use to boost output.

exhibits.title: Employee Survey — Hours per Activity by Group
exhibits.shows: A table from an employee survey showing how many hours each of three groups of 5 employees (15 total) takes to complete each of the three shoemaking tasks: cutting, stitching, and finishing.

framework: Understand the current production process end-to-end (stages, time per stage, number of workers)
Identify constraints: no new hires available, no new technology
Analyze labor utilization: are workers deployed optimally across tasks?
Identify skill differentiation across workers (use Exhibit 1)
Evaluate specialization as a lever: assign each group to its best task
Quantify the impact of specialization on output (hours per pair, weekly output)

questions.prompt: What insight does Exhibit 1 reveal about how workers should be deployed?
questions.guidance: The candidate should observe that each group has a comparative advantage in one task: Group 1 is fastest at cutting (3 hrs), Group 3 is fastest at stitching (3 hrs), and Group 2 is fastest at finishing (3 hrs). By specializing each group in its strongest task, the total time per pair of shoes drops from 12 hours to 9 hours (3+3+3), increasing throughput without adding labor or changing quality.

questions.prompt: Under the new specialized system, what is the maximum weekly output?
questions.guidance: Calculate total available labor hours per week, divide by 9 hours per pair per worker, then multiply by 15 workers.

math.setup: Hours per pair (new system) = 9. Each employee works 9 hours/day x 5 days/week = 45 hours/week. Output per employee per week = 45 / 9 = 5 pairs. Total weekly output = 5 pairs x 15 employees = 75 pairs.
steps: Hours per week per employee: 9 hrs/day x 5 days = 45 hrs
Output per employee per week: 45 / 9 = 5 pairs

questions.prompt: What is the total weekly profit under the new system?
questions.guidance: Use the given price and cost data to compute gross profit per pair, total gross profit, then subtract labor and fixed costs.

math.setup: Price = $300/pair. Material cost = $40/pair. Shipping = $10/pair. Variable cost per pair = $50. Gross profit per pair = $250. Weekly output = 75 pairs. Total gross profit = 75 x $250 = $18,750. Total employee hours per week = 15 employees x 45 hrs = 675 hrs. Employee cost = 675 x $15/hr = $10,125. Fixed costs = $1,000/week. Weekly profit = $18,750 - $10,125 - $1,000 = $7,625.

recommendation: Change the production process so that each group of employees specializes in a single task: Group 1 handles cutting, Group 3 handles stitching, and Group 2 handles finishing.

This specialization reduces the average time per pair of shoes from 12 hours to 9 hours, enabling the client to increase weekly output from approximately 56 pairs to 75 pairs using the same 15 workers — a ~33% increase — without compromising quality.
risks: Employees may resist the change; those accustomed to crafting full pairs end-to-end may experience morale or engagement issues.
There may be one-time implementation costs, such as rearranging the workshop layout to support an assembly-line style workflow.
Any heavily entrenched process change carries execution risk during the transition period.
next_steps: Pilot the specialized workflow with a small group first to validate the time savings and identify implementation hiccups before full rollout.
Monitor quality metrics closely during and after the transition to ensure the change does not introduce new defects.
Consider phased rollout to smooth implementation and allow workers time to adjust to their specialized roles.
